tells: Real simulation work: liquid and glass caustics, refraction in the lens shells, and a fluid that holds its shape while fracturing. None of it looks like stock primitives
The product is rendered as material: the glasses are recast as a translucent, organic, almost anatomical form (frames 3–4), which is a genuine transformation rather than a static packshot
Shot scale varies a lot: extreme macro fluid, a hero product shot, a frontal icon and a cellular/neural abstraction, which suggests a built arc from chaos to product to 'evolution'

Against it: a monochrome electric-blue CG-liquid look is a well-worn tech-launch genre; 'XREAL ... 1S' set wide apart in a default grotesk and a tracked-out 'E V O L U T I O N' are standard launch-film type
Overall this reads as polished commercial CGI studio work, not an AI tool: geometry stays consistent from shot to shot and the product detail is accurate
gaps: The idea is a genre convention (product born from liquid); it needs a concept specific to AR glasses, such as seeing or overlaying worlds, instead of generic 'fluid evolution'

The single-hue blue grade flattens every shot into the same mood; it needs a counter-colour or a shift in light temperature across the arc to give the film structure and memorability

tells: One committed system: every image (a running figure, a coin in a vortex, an orbiting planet, padlocks, a grid of spinning coins) is built from ASCII glyphs, so the type is the image

The ASCII medium fits the subject: payment and crypto infrastructure rendered as code and characters, with fake source code ('matchcut_engine.h', 'StartDirectPayment()') used as texture and as narrative
Tightly limited ultramarine-and-white palette held with discipline; density changes in the glyph fields create depth and flow lines

Choreography is visible: glyph fields stream directionally (the <<< arrows), the planet's orbit ring carries the label 'Faster', and the coin grid shows staggered rotation phases, which implies careful timing
Weaknesses: ASCII art is a known trend, the pixel figure and padlocks are a bit literal (security = padlock), and the white label chips ('Crypto is...') feel UI-like
gaps: The metaphors are literal: padlock for security, coins for crypto. It needs one surprising image only ASCII could produce, rather than ASCII renderings of stock icons
There is little tonal or lighting variation; adding glyph weight and size contrast, or a second colour state, would create a dramatic peak the way C's flare-lit title reveal does
The white tag labels read as placeholder UI; the copy needs a typographic treatment as ambitious as the glyph system around it

tells: The idea is specific and unrepeatable: the story's world as a clockwork map whose cities mechanically build themselves, and it doubles as a navigational tool for the series
Real material and light: an engraved armillary band lit by a sun-flare, aged brass, wood and parchment textures, and a tilt-shift miniature depth of field that sells the scale
The credits are integrated into the world: a small sigil-plus-Trajan-style serif tucked into the terrain rather than overlaid. The main title is set inside the astrolabe band with flanking beasts

Every frame works as a poster, and the choreography is clear: the camera travels across the map, mechanisms rise, a needle and pin locate King's Landing, and the title lockup bookends the opening flare
The palette moves deliberately between warm brass and gold, cool slate and parchment green
gaps: The map's diagrammatic overview frame is the least textured moment; it could carry more of the material richness of the mechanism shots
The credit type is very small against busy detail, so legibility depends on the camera holding still
The main-title lockup leans on familiar fantasy-epic conventions (flare, Trajan-like serif) where the rest of the piece is invented

tells: A textbook automated/template kinetic-type promo: a heavy default grotesk (Inter-like display weight) with a tiny tracked mono label ('ROP 0 1 21', '11.21 — 09:00 CET')
A single red accent used as an underline in nearly every frame; speed lines behind 'FAST' are the most literal visualisation possible
Three of five frames are the same centred word-on-a-flat-field layout with the words swapped ('VELO', 'VELO 9', 'VELO 9' plus date); a slide-deck structure
The countdown-dial '9' is a stock radial-tick motif; there is no light, texture, material or depth anywhere
Nothing a viewer would remember: product name plus number plus launch date, with no image, no subject and no point of view
gaps: It has no idea: it needs a concept beyond the name, the word 'fast' and a date, such as a world or metaphor specific to the product, the way C builds a mechanical map
The typography needs a point of view: a custom or characterful face, real scale contrast and interaction with image instead of a centred bold sans with an underline
It needs image, material and light (real texture, depth, a palette beyond black, cream and red) plus varied compositions so the frames progress instead of repeating one layout

defects: Mono labels reveal as broken partial strings ('ROP 0  1  21', '1 21 — 09:0  CE'). This typewriter or scramble mid-state reads as dropped glyphs, not as an intended effect.

The spec-sheet layout leaves the right 60% of the frame empty except for small tracked labels, and the stat numbers sit almost on the left edge ('182g' is clipped near x=0). The numbers have no margin.
The stat transition is a hard vertical bar-wipe on top of numbers that are still counting ('140g/74%' under the bars). Two systems fight in the same frame and the wipe has no easing hierarchy.
The FAST speed lines are stock horizontal dashes that layer over and through the letterforms with no occlusion logic. They read as a template motion-lines preset.
The dial shot is a static radial tick graphic with a centred '9'. Its tick lengths are uneven and the inner ring is irregular, so it looks procedurally generated rather than drawn.
The last ~1 s is near-static (change per second 7.6). The hold is earned as a lock-up, but nothing breathes in it: no settle and no secondary motion.
Everything is flat vector with no grain, light or depth cue. At 100% the edges are clean but there is no material to the finish.
gaps: There is no single motion idea carrying the film. Five unrelated generic moves (underline grow, skew plus speed lines, radial dial, number count with bar-wipe, underline lock-up) are cut together, and none of them hands off its momentum or geometry into the next shot.

Weight and easing are thin. The only physical cue is the FAST skew, with no overshoot, drag or follow-through on the heavy grotesk. Top studio work would let 'velocity' deform and spring the type itself and carry motion blur through the cuts.

The finish and composition are template-grade. There is no texture, light or camera, and the frames are lopsided (empty right halves, partially revealed mono text). Only the opening and closing lock-ups hold up as stills.
